docs.text: Task owns operation identity and outcome; RunStatistics owns operation timing and report publication. It references the existing options and pipeline owners. Pipeline and PipelineStep own all pipeline/worker timing samples and progress. Summary dictionaries are one-way output adapters: they never replace or mutate the owner's samples. Server progress is read from that owner without a second cached progress state. Actual executor counts also come from dispatch-owned resource fields rather than a separate calculation in the reporter. VolumeCache , CloudVolumeInterface , BoundingBox , and the native TIFF inspector own geometry and effective volume metadata. Downloads and reporting share download_volume_geometry . The volume reporting snapshot is a one-way serialization boundary before cleanup, never an input to scientific execution. Output naming, atomic file publication, Docker export, and recovery extend the existing file/volume facilities. The memory collector extends this same lifecycle. The fixed-local-source benchmark and reproducible commands are documented in the benchmark guide . The owner-approved 1% combined in-operation engineering target applies to longer runs, assessed alongside inter-run variability and fixed startup/shutdown costs. For the recorded #139 real-data evidence, acceptance is scoped to the long Salivary Duct path; short-path costs remain reported and are not a general 1% guarantee. RAM collection shares the budget with timing and volume reporting. The real-data comparison uses the canonical data-step duration, retaining worker/ manager startup and shutdown inside that step. Earlier preparation, sampler startup/shutdown and final reporting are excluded. These measurements do not isolate every cause of a timing difference; negative changes reflect variation, not free instrumentation. Two pairs do not establish a statistical upper bound.
docs.title: Verification and ownership

docs.text: The collector belongs to RunStatistics and runs only around Pipeline.process . It stops before volume inspection, output transfer, cleanup and report delivery. Each operation starts a fresh sampling window and uses the same run identifier, status and report delivery as its timing statistics. No container-lifetime peak or host free-memory delta is attributed to a run. Backend execution OS Metric Source and coverage Linux, including Docker on any host process_tree_nonshmem_pss_plus_managed_resident_bytes Sum of /proc/<pid>/smaps_rollup Pss - Pss_Shmem , plus mincore residency of each live managed shared segment once Native Windows (64-bit) process_tree_private_resident_plus_managed_allocated_bytes Sum of PROCESS_MEMORY_COUNTERS_EX2.PrivateWorkingSetSize , plus the size of each live managed allocation once Native macOS process_tree_private_plus_managed_resident_bytes libproc private resident pages, excluding the manager's owned segment ranges, plus mincore residency of each live managed segment once Linux removes the process counter's entire shared-memory PSS contribution before adding managed residency. This avoids counting a managed page again when it has only one reader. Reading the backing object's residency also includes resident managed buffers queued after their producer closes, before another process has accessed them. Shared-memory segments outside the manager's ownership are not added back. Other shared memory, such as fork-shared anonymous pages and mapped files, retains the OS's proportional accounting. Windows uses one private working-set counter per process instead of enumerating its working-set pages. Its managed term is allocated bytes, not resident bytes : unused, paged-out or otherwise nonresident parts of live allocations remain included. The metric name makes this distinction explicit. The counter requires 64-bit Python and Windows 10 or 11 version 22H2 with the September 2023 update or later. Missing counter support makes the metric unavailable; it does not silently fall back to the old working-set scan. macOS retains a libproc region walk for private residency. A segment can appear private when the manager is its only mapper, so the manager's ranges are excluded before managed residency is added. Compressed/swapped pages are not included. Native CI exercises the macOS reader and short collector lifecycle. Native macOS slice/backprojection performance and macOS-host Docker delivery are deferred on #139; focused CI does not replace those workflow checks. There is no separate TIFF or resident file-cache accounting. Ordinary mapped-file pages may still contribute to the native process counter; cached pages absent from process mappings are not added separately. The platform metrics differ in how they treat shared pages and, on Windows, managed allocation residency. They must not be treated as interchangeable measurements of exactly the same RAM. The scope includes the backend parent, discovered workers and helpers, including the shared-memory manager. It excludes the sampler itself. Parent state can predate the operation. Concurrent operations in the same server share the parent and descendants, so overlapping records describe overlapping process trees, not isolated per-job allocations . A descendant already observed remains in scope if it is subsequently reparented. Children born and gone between samples can be missed. Psutil Process equality and hashing are the sole runtime process identity, including PID-reuse protection; public create_time() values are not identity keys. On Linux and macOS those wall-clock timestamps can change after a clock adjustment even while the same process is running. The host OS remains unknown from inside Docker; the selected metric follows the execution OS in environment.os . A small separate interpreter performs collection, avoiding a sampler thread in the parent before Linux forks workers. The manager's existing _segments registry remains the sole owner of live allocation handles and release policy. At allocation, registration and release boundaries, it publishes a derived snapshot of names and sizes, plus its own mapping addresses on macOS. Overlapping runs share one observation session. Manager startup receives that session through its existing initializer seam; workers and array attachments need no observation context, mapping registry or TIFF wrappers. Snapshots and sampler-control files are one-way observation/IPC adapters. They never supply allocation or lifecycle state back to the manager. POSIX residency queries temporarily open a read-only mapping without faulting in the buffer or acquiring unlink authority. A manager started before an observation session is not retroactively observed. The scientific pipelines start their managers inside the collection window. Disabled reporting creates no sampler or observation workspace. The narrow identity adapter in common/memory_ipc.py serializes the validated private Process._ident value together with the psutil version and platform. It matches incoming identities against live Process objects at the IPC boundary; serialized values do not become a second runtime identity registry. Missing, unsupported, or unverified identity data makes the affected measurement unavailable rather than falling back to a PID or public creation timestamp, or treating an unverified manager as owning no segments. Psutil is pinned to 7.1.3 in package metadata as well as the Poetry lock, covering pip/wheel installations and both Docker build paths. This private-API dependency must be reviewed before changing that pin: Linux, Windows and macOS identity/IPC compatibility tests and the clock-adjustment regressions must pass for the proposed version. Supported runtime identity comes from psutil itself; Ouroboros does not maintain an alternative platform identity calculation. Liveness checks likewise validate a fresh psutil identity before comparing it with the retained Process : unreadable identity is unknown coverage, not proof that the worker exited. Discovery still uses psutil's children() implementation; in 7.1.3 a backwards clock adjustment within one enumeration can omit a previously unseen child because psutil itself filters by public creation timestamps. Retained workers are checked independently, but sampling is not a complete process census. status is sampled when all admitted sweeps succeeded, partial when some failed, unavailable when none completed, or not_started if the pipeline was never reached. Process or allocation changes during a sweep make that sweep incomplete. Manifest reads and publication reuse the control-file retry for Windows sharing violations (up to 0.5 seconds, 10 ms spacing). Persistent failures remain explicit. A failed manager-manifest publication invalidates the metric rather than silently omitting managed allocations. The peak is the maximum complete sampled tree total , not an OS high-water mark or a sum of independently observed process peaks. Reads within a sweep are sequential, not an atomic tree snapshot. Sampling may miss short-lived peaks; external processes sharing pages affect Linux PSS. Sweeps crossing the end of the operation are discarded. Requested and observed intervals, sweep cost, complete and incomplete counts and errors accompany the result. No complete sample means an unavailable value, never a successful zero. The default interval is one second; collection cost is assessed against combined reporting overhead. last_complete_sample_bytes is the last admitted complete sample, not a live reading at report publication. sampling gives the window length, first and last admitted sweep offsets, requested interval, observed start-to-start interval range, and discarded/incomplete/complete counts. collector_cpu_seconds includes polling and completion of an in-flight sweep discarded at stop; max_sweep_seconds includes discarded sweeps too. These costs diagnose the observer; only an external pipeline timer measures in-operation overhead. The native CI matrix covers Linux, Windows and Apple Silicon macOS on Python 3.11 and 3.12. The current simplification is checked with focused ownership, accounting and reporting tests; it has not repeated the long real-data benchmark campaign. Historical Linux and Windows pipeline results, component diagnostics, and Docker/frozen-executable checks are retained in the benchmark guide . Those results describe earlier collectors. In particular, the earlier Windows long-path overhead finding applies to the removed working-set enumeration and mapping-tracking implementation, not a measurement of this replacement. Focused tests do not establish a 1% overhead bound or native macOS pipeline acceptance. No cross-platform 1% guarantee is claimed. The clock-dependent identity defect in #162 invalidates the affected RAM results; fixing identity does not retroactively repair those reports. Fresh long-run overhead acceptance is tracked separately in #163 , and replacement publication measurements remain with the publication. The native macOS pipeline and macOS-host Docker deferrals on #139 remain unchanged.

docs.text: Technical Constants This page documents hardcoded implementation limits that affect Ouroboros behavior at runtime. Values here are extracted directly from the shipping source. If you change them locally, update this page in the same commit. File explorer All file explorer limits live in src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts at the top of the file, alongside the shared teardown delay in src/shared/constants.ts . They apply to the per-directory non-recursive watchers with lazy expansion that back the File Explorer panel in the Electron app. Starting with #110 , the file explorer no longer opens a single recursive watcher on the selected root. Instead, the main process keeps one non-recursive watcher per directory the user has currently expanded, plus one for the root. Expanding a subfolder starts a new watcher for it; collapsing schedules teardown after COLLAPSE_TEARDOWN_DELAY_MS , so quick collapse-then-reopen costs nothing. Watcher path-count limit Symbol: FILE_EXPLORER_WATCH_LIMIT Value: 100_000 Source: src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts line 9 Reported inside every folder-contents-error payload. Why it exists. Every watcher mirrors its discovered paths into renderer state. Even with lazy expansion, an aggressive user could open a handful of dense subfolders in sequence and still exhaust memory. One hundred thousand visible paths is the ceiling picked in [#104][pr-104] as a balance between usefulness for typical scan/output folders and keeping the renderer well under its default 4 GB heap. Role change from #110. Before #110 this was the underlying watcher package's per-watcher limit . Under the lazy model it is instead an aggregate session budget summed across every currently open watcher; a watcher's contribution is reclaimed when its folder is collapsed and torn down. Second role from #111. The same constant caps the plugin-facing get-folder-contents one-shot enumeration used by the request-directory-contents iframe message (see the plugins guide ). A plugin's recursive walk stops when the enumeration hits the cap; the response is returned with error.code: 'limit' and error.truncated: true , and nodes holds the partial result already gathered. Enumeration and watcher budgets are counted separately (the enumeration count is per-request and does not accumulate across requests), so a plugin cannot starve the file explorer by issuing many recursive requests. User-visible behavior when reached. Once the aggregate visible add count crosses the limit, the main process emits folder-contents-error with a message of the form File explorer stopped loading after 100000 visible paths across all open folders. Choose a smaller folder or expand the folder in smaller pieces. The existing renderer alert system surfaces this as a warning toast. Further add events for that session are not attributed to the counter but already loaded paths remain visible. When to reconsider. Raise this only after profiling shows headroom in both the main watchers and the renderer heap for your typical workload. Lower it if you routinely work on constrained machines and want the warning to appear sooner. Watcher teardown delay after collapse Symbol: COLLAPSE_TEARDOWN_DELAY_MS Value: 30_000 (milliseconds) Source: src/shared/constants.ts Why it exists. Collapsing a folder in the file explorer should not immediately close its watcher and drop its renderer state, because users routinely collapse-then-reopen the same folder while navigating. The delay makes that pattern free: as long as the user re-expands within thirty seconds, no watcher churn and no state re-fetch happen. After the delay elapses, the main process closes the non-recursive watcher on the collapsed subfolder and the renderer prunes its children from state. Root's watcher is exempt - collapsing root is a no-op; root's watcher only closes when a new root is opened or the window is torn down. User-visible behavior when reached. Nothing visible changes at the moment of teardown. The collapsed folder's shell remains rendered; its children have already stopped rendering visually because of the collapse. Re-expanding after teardown behaves like a fresh expand: the main process starts a new watcher and streams the initial batch back into the renderer's state. When to reconsider. Shorten if renderer memory pressure from still-cached collapsed subtrees is a problem. Lengthen if users complain that re-opening a folder after a long detour repopulates it visibly. Update batch size Symbol: FILE_EXPLORER_UPDATE_BATCH_LIMIT Value: 500 Source: src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts line 10 Why it exists. [#105][pr-105] introduced batching so that a large initial folder scan no longer produces one IPC message and one React state update per discovered path. Five hundred events per batch amortizes the IPC round-trip and lets the renderer apply the whole batch inside a single setNodes call. User-visible behavior when reached. As soon as five hundred watcher events have accumulated in the main process, the pending queue is flushed immediately over the folder-contents-update-batch IPC channel instead of waiting for the flush interval below. The File Explorer panel then updates once for the whole batch. When to reconsider. Increase the batch size if profiling shows IPC or React reconciliation is still the bottleneck on very large folders. Decrease it if you see visible latency between file system changes and the first batch appearing in the panel. Update flush interval Symbol: FILE_EXPLORER_UPDATE_INTERVAL_MS Value: 100 (milliseconds) Source: src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts line 11 Why it exists. The batch flush also runs on a timer so that small bursts of changes still reach the renderer promptly, even when the five-hundred-event threshold above is never hit. User-visible behavior when reached. Any queued events are flushed at most one hundred milliseconds after the first event in the queue was enqueued. The panel therefore feels responsive to individual file create/delete events while still coalescing large scans. When to reconsider. Shorten the interval if the panel feels laggy during light file activity. Lengthen it if renderer CPU during heavy scans is a problem and you would rather trade responsiveness for throughput. Plugin directory broadcast Broadcast payload: { directoryPath, directoryName, nodes: {} } Source: src/renderer/src/contexts/IFrameContext.tsx ( broadcastDirectoryContext ) Why it exists. Before [#106][pr-106], every directory context change posted the full recursive nodes tree into each plugin iframe. For the same large folders that motivated [#51][issue-51] this cloned the entire file tree on every update and stacked on top of the watcher and renderer costs above. User-visible behavior. Plugins still receive the selected directory path and name through the existing send-directory-contents message. The nodes field is present for shape compatibility but is always an empty object. Plugins that need to browse the directory tree use the request-directory-contents / send-directory-contents-response message pair added in [#111][issue-111] (see the plugins guide ) rather than depending on this broadcast payload. When to reconsider. Do not restore the full-tree broadcast without first landing a memory-safe, on-demand alternative. The on-demand API from #111 is that alternative; prefer extending it over resurrecting the broadcast. Main process (Electron) Plugin file server port Symbol: PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT Value: 3000 (default) Source: src/main/servers/file-server.ts line 7 Environment override: OUROBOROS_PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT (integer; unset, empty, or non-numeric values fall back to 3000 ) Why it exists. The main process forks a local Express + serve-static worker (see resources/processes/file-server-script.mjs ) that serves every installed plugin's static assets over http://127.0.0.1:3000/ by default. The renderer and plugin iframes load their index.html , icons, and any bundled JS from this server. User-visible behavior. If another process on the host is already listening on the chosen port the fork fails and plugins load with broken assets. There is no automatic fallback beyond the env override. When to reconsider. Set OUROBOROS_PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT when 3000 conflicts with a different local service. The renderer discovers the URL through getPluginFileServerURL() , so the port change is picked up without touching any user-facing setting. Landed in [PR #109][pr-109]. Docker volume server port Symbol: VOLUME_SERVER_PORT Value: 3001 (default) Source: src/main/servers/volume-server.ts line 7 Environment override: OUROBOROS_VOLUME_SERVER_PORT (integer; unset, empty, or non-numeric values fall back to 3001 ) Why it exists. The volume server is a second forked Node process (see resources/processes/volume-server-script.mjs ) that shells out to docker run --rm commands so that host files can be copied into and out of the ouroboros-volume Docker named volume. The main server container reaches back to it through http://host.docker.internal:3001 (see Python server below). User-visible behavior. Copy-to-volume and copy-to-host requests fail if the chosen port is busy or if Docker is not available. Plugin data transfer into the shared volume breaks in that case. When to reconsider. Set OUROBOROS_VOLUME_SERVER_PORT when 3001 conflicts locally. Keep the Python-side default in sync ( VOLUME_SERVER_URL in python/ouroboros/common/volume_server_interface.py ); the Python side is still hard-coded to 3001 because the container reaches the host over host.docker.internal where the port is independent of any host-side conflict. Landed in [PR #109][pr-109]. Docker volume name Symbol: VOLUME Value: 'ouroboros-volume' Source: src/main/servers/volume-server.ts line 9, matched by the volumes.ouroboros-volume.name entry in python/compose.yml , python/compose.dev.yml , and the compose file written by scripts/prepare-production-server.mjs . Why it exists. The Python server, the volume server helper, and the main process all address the same Docker named volume so that plugin uploads land where the pipeline can read them. Invariant. The literal string 'ouroboros-volume' is duplicated across four call sites: src/main/servers/volume-server.ts , python/ouroboros/common/volume_server_interface.py , python/compose.yml , python/compose.dev.yml , and the compose file written by scripts/prepare-production-server.mjs . Docker Compose YAML is required to be static, so a single source of truth would need a code-generation step the team has not opted into; the invariant lives in this documentation and in code review discipline. If you rename this value in one place, every listed file must move with it in the same commit. User-visible behavior. On app shutdown the volume server helper issues docker run --rm ... rm -rf /volume/* against this named volume. Anything else stored under the same volume name is deleted. When to reconsider. Rename it if you need to run multiple Ouroboros installs against the same Docker daemon without stomping each other's volumes. All call sites listed above must agree. Renderer Server connection settings Symbols: DEFAULT_SERVER_URL , retryDelay Values: DEFAULT_SERVER_URL = 'http://127.0.0.1:8000' retryDelay = 5000 (milliseconds) Source: src/renderer/src/contexts/ServerContext.tsx lines 4 and 41 Why it exists. DEFAULT_SERVER_URL is the base URL the renderer uses for all REST and SSE calls to the Python server. retryDelay is the interval at which the checkServerStatus loop pings that base URL to update the connected flag driving the ProgressPanel status. User-visible behavior. The "connected" indicator can lag reality by up to about five seconds. Any fetch or stream started while the app thinks the server is down is placed on fetchQueue and replayed once the health poll flips to connected . When to reconsider. Lower retryDelay for a snappier connection indicator at the cost of extra HTTP traffic. Change DEFAULT_SERVER_URL if you point Ouroboros at a remote server, but keep it aligned with the Python-side HOST / PORT defaults documented below. IFrame plugin allowed origins Symbol: allowedHostnames Value: ['localhost', '127.0.0.1', '0.0.0.0'] Source: src/renderer/src/contexts/IFrameContext.tsx line 30 Why it exists. The renderer only dispatches read-file , save-file , and register-plugin messages from iframes whose event.origin parses to a URL whose hostname is exactly one of these values. Plugin content is served locally through the plugin file server (see PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT , default port 3000), so all legitimate origins are loopback. Any port on those hosts is accepted; the port itself is env-configurable. Security note. The previous implementation used text.startsWith(item) , which would accept attacker-controlled hosts such as http://localhost.evil.example . The current implementation parses event.origin with new URL(...) and compares hostname for exact equality; malformed origins fall through to a deny. Landed in [PR #109][pr-109]. User-visible behavior. Any plugin iframe served from a non-loopback origin is silently ignored: its messages never trigger file reads, writes, or registration. When to reconsider. Add an entry only if you deliberately host plugin content off-device (for example, over https:// to a controlled host). Broadening this list widens the file-read and file-write surface exposed to third-party pages, and non-loopback additions should use exact origin equality against a full URL, not just a hostname. Slice visualization sampling ratio Symbol: SLICE_RENDER_PROPORTION Value: 0.008 Source: src/renderer/src/routes/SlicesPage/SlicesPage.tsx line 26 Why it exists. The 3D slice preview draws only every Nth rectangle where N = floor(rects.length * 0.008) . This keeps very long paths (tens of thousands of rects) from stalling the WebGL scene. User-visible behavior. For a 10 000-rect path this renders roughly 125 rectangles: enough to convey the shape of the sweep without freezing the visualization. Fewer rects than about 125 render every rect. When to reconsider. Raise it to see more slices in the preview at the cost of frame rate; lower it if the preview lags on very long paths. Python server Server host and port Symbols: HOST , PORT , DOCKER_HOST , DOCKER_PORT Values (defaults): HOST = '127.0.0.1' PORT = 8000 DOCKER_HOST = '0.0.0.0' DOCKER_PORT = 8000 Source: [ python/ouroboros/common/server.py ][py-server] lines 10-14 Environment overrides: OUROBOROS_SERVER_HOST -> HOST OUROBOROS_SERVER_PORT -> PORT (integer) OUROBOROS_DOCKER_SERVER_HOST -> DOCKER_HOST OUROBOROS_DOCKER_SERVER_PORT -> DOCKER_PORT (integer) Why it exists. The desktop-only server entry point ( ouroboros-server ) binds Uvicorn to loopback, while the containerised server entry point ( ouroboros-docker-server ) binds to all interfaces so the host can reach the container through the compose 8000:8000 port mapping. User-visible behavior. The renderer's DEFAULT_SERVER_URL above assumes port 8000. Changing PORT (or OUROBOROS_SERVER_PORT ) or the compose port mapping without updating the renderer breaks the client. When to reconsider. Set the env overrides if you need to expose the desktop server to another machine (rare) or if 8000 conflicts with another service. Update DEFAULT_SERVER_URL in the renderer and the compose port mapping in the same commit. Landed in [PR #109][pr-109]. Volume server URL (Python side) Symbols: VOLUME_SERVER_URL , PLUGIN_NAME Values: VOLUME_SERVER_URL = 'http://host.docker.internal:3001' PLUGIN_NAME = 'main' Source: python/ouroboros/common/volume_server_interface.py lines 3-4 Why it exists. From inside the server container, the volume server running on the host is reached through the Docker special DNS name host.docker.internal , mapped in each compose file via extra_hosts: - "host.docker.internal:host-gateway" . PLUGIN_NAME is the fixed subfolder on the shared volume used by the main pipeline. Why 'main'. Ouroboros is the main application of its own plugin ecosystem, so the Python side treats itself as the always- main plugin when addressing paths on the shared volume. There is no planned per-plugin path scheme on the Python side; plugin content is scoped by the Electron-side plugin folder, not by a Python-visible slug. PLUGIN_NAME therefore stays a constant rather than a parameter. User-visible behavior. If the compose file omits the host.docker.internal extra host, or if the Electron main process is not running the volume server, requests time out and plugin/data transfer into the volume fails. When to reconsider. Change the URL only in coordination with the Electron-side VOLUME_SERVER_PORT in src/main/servers/volume-server.ts . docs.text: This page documents hardcoded implementation limits that affect Ouroboros behavior at runtime. Values here are extracted directly from the shipping source. If you change them locally, update this page in the same commit.
docs.title: Technical Constants

docs.text: All file explorer limits live in src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts at the top of the file, alongside the shared teardown delay in src/shared/constants.ts . They apply to the per-directory non-recursive watchers with lazy expansion that back the File Explorer panel in the Electron app. Starting with #110 , the file explorer no longer opens a single recursive watcher on the selected root. Instead, the main process keeps one non-recursive watcher per directory the user has currently expanded, plus one for the root. Expanding a subfolder starts a new watcher for it; collapsing schedules teardown after COLLAPSE_TEARDOWN_DELAY_MS , so quick collapse-then-reopen costs nothing.
docs.title: File explorer

docs.text: Symbol: FILE_EXPLORER_WATCH_LIMIT Value: 100_000 Source: src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts line 9 Reported inside every folder-contents-error payload. Why it exists. Every watcher mirrors its discovered paths into renderer state. Even with lazy expansion, an aggressive user could open a handful of dense subfolders in sequence and still exhaust memory. One hundred thousand visible paths is the ceiling picked in [#104][pr-104] as a balance between usefulness for typical scan/output folders and keeping the renderer well under its default 4 GB heap. Role change from #110. Before #110 this was the underlying watcher package's per-watcher limit . Under the lazy model it is instead an aggregate session budget summed across every currently open watcher; a watcher's contribution is reclaimed when its folder is collapsed and torn down. Second role from #111. The same constant caps the plugin-facing get-folder-contents one-shot enumeration used by the request-directory-contents iframe message (see the plugins guide ). A plugin's recursive walk stops when the enumeration hits the cap; the response is returned with error.code: 'limit' and error.truncated: true , and nodes holds the partial result already gathered. Enumeration and watcher budgets are counted separately (the enumeration count is per-request and does not accumulate across requests), so a plugin cannot starve the file explorer by issuing many recursive requests. User-visible behavior when reached. Once the aggregate visible add count crosses the limit, the main process emits folder-contents-error with a message of the form File explorer stopped loading after 100000 visible paths across all open folders. Choose a smaller folder or expand the folder in smaller pieces. The existing renderer alert system surfaces this as a warning toast. Further add events for that session are not attributed to the counter but already loaded paths remain visible. When to reconsider. Raise this only after profiling shows headroom in both the main watchers and the renderer heap for your typical workload. Lower it if you routinely work on constrained machines and want the warning to appear sooner.
docs.title: Watcher path-count limit

docs.text: Symbol: COLLAPSE_TEARDOWN_DELAY_MS Value: 30_000 (milliseconds) Source: src/shared/constants.ts Why it exists. Collapsing a folder in the file explorer should not immediately close its watcher and drop its renderer state, because users routinely collapse-then-reopen the same folder while navigating. The delay makes that pattern free: as long as the user re-expands within thirty seconds, no watcher churn and no state re-fetch happen. After the delay elapses, the main process closes the non-recursive watcher on the collapsed subfolder and the renderer prunes its children from state. Root's watcher is exempt - collapsing root is a no-op; root's watcher only closes when a new root is opened or the window is torn down. User-visible behavior when reached. Nothing visible changes at the moment of teardown. The collapsed folder's shell remains rendered; its children have already stopped rendering visually because of the collapse. Re-expanding after teardown behaves like a fresh expand: the main process starts a new watcher and streams the initial batch back into the renderer's state. When to reconsider. Shorten if renderer memory pressure from still-cached collapsed subtrees is a problem. Lengthen if users complain that re-opening a folder after a long detour repopulates it visibly.
docs.title: Watcher teardown delay after collapse

docs.text: Symbol: FILE_EXPLORER_UPDATE_BATCH_LIMIT Value: 500 Source: src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts line 10 Why it exists. [#105][pr-105] introduced batching so that a large initial folder scan no longer produces one IPC message and one React state update per discovered path. Five hundred events per batch amortizes the IPC round-trip and lets the renderer apply the whole batch inside a single setNodes call. User-visible behavior when reached. As soon as five hundred watcher events have accumulated in the main process, the pending queue is flushed immediately over the folder-contents-update-batch IPC channel instead of waiting for the flush interval below. The File Explorer panel then updates once for the whole batch. When to reconsider. Increase the batch size if profiling shows IPC or React reconciliation is still the bottleneck on very large folders. Decrease it if you see visible latency between file system changes and the first batch appearing in the panel.
docs.title: Update batch size

docs.text: Symbol: FILE_EXPLORER_UPDATE_INTERVAL_MS Value: 100 (milliseconds) Source: src/main/event-handlers/filesystem.ts line 11 Why it exists. The batch flush also runs on a timer so that small bursts of changes still reach the renderer promptly, even when the five-hundred-event threshold above is never hit. User-visible behavior when reached. Any queued events are flushed at most one hundred milliseconds after the first event in the queue was enqueued. The panel therefore feels responsive to individual file create/delete events while still coalescing large scans. When to reconsider. Shorten the interval if the panel feels laggy during light file activity. Lengthen it if renderer CPU during heavy scans is a problem and you would rather trade responsiveness for throughput.
docs.title: Update flush interval

docs.text: Broadcast payload: { directoryPath, directoryName, nodes: {} } Source: src/renderer/src/contexts/IFrameContext.tsx ( broadcastDirectoryContext ) Why it exists. Before [#106][pr-106], every directory context change posted the full recursive nodes tree into each plugin iframe. For the same large folders that motivated [#51][issue-51] this cloned the entire file tree on every update and stacked on top of the watcher and renderer costs above. User-visible behavior. Plugins still receive the selected directory path and name through the existing send-directory-contents message. The nodes field is present for shape compatibility but is always an empty object. Plugins that need to browse the directory tree use the request-directory-contents / send-directory-contents-response message pair added in [#111][issue-111] (see the plugins guide ) rather than depending on this broadcast payload. When to reconsider. Do not restore the full-tree broadcast without first landing a memory-safe, on-demand alternative. The on-demand API from #111 is that alternative; prefer extending it over resurrecting the broadcast.
docs.title: Plugin directory broadcast

docs.text: Symbol: PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT Value: 3000 (default) Source: src/main/servers/file-server.ts line 7 Environment override: OUROBOROS_PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT (integer; unset, empty, or non-numeric values fall back to 3000 ) Why it exists. The main process forks a local Express + serve-static worker (see resources/processes/file-server-script.mjs ) that serves every installed plugin's static assets over http://127.0.0.1:3000/ by default. The renderer and plugin iframes load their index.html , icons, and any bundled JS from this server. User-visible behavior. If another process on the host is already listening on the chosen port the fork fails and plugins load with broken assets. There is no automatic fallback beyond the env override. When to reconsider. Set OUROBOROS_PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT when 3000 conflicts with a different local service. The renderer discovers the URL through getPluginFileServerURL() , so the port change is picked up without touching any user-facing setting. Landed in [PR #109][pr-109].
docs.title: Plugin file server port

docs.text: Symbol: VOLUME_SERVER_PORT Value: 3001 (default) Source: src/main/servers/volume-server.ts line 7 Environment override: OUROBOROS_VOLUME_SERVER_PORT (integer; unset, empty, or non-numeric values fall back to 3001 ) Why it exists. The volume server is a second forked Node process (see resources/processes/volume-server-script.mjs ) that shells out to docker run --rm commands so that host files can be copied into and out of the ouroboros-volume Docker named volume. The main server container reaches back to it through http://host.docker.internal:3001 (see Python server below). User-visible behavior. Copy-to-volume and copy-to-host requests fail if the chosen port is busy or if Docker is not available. Plugin data transfer into the shared volume breaks in that case. When to reconsider. Landed in [PR #109][pr-109].

DEFAULT_SERVER_URL is the base URL the renderer uses for all REST and SSE calls to the Python server. retryDelay is the interval at which the checkServerStatus loop pings that base URL to update the connected flag driving the ProgressPanel status. User-visible behavior. The "connected" indicator can lag reality by up to about five seconds. Any fetch or stream started while the app thinks the server is down is placed on fetchQueue and replayed once the health poll flips to connected . When to reconsider. Lower retryDelay for a snappier connection indicator at the cost of extra HTTP traffic. Change DEFAULT_SERVER_URL if you point Ouroboros at a remote server, but keep it aligned with the Python-side HOST / PORT defaults documented below.

docs.text: Symbol: allowedHostnames Value: ['localhost', '127.0.0.1', '0.0.0.0'] Source: src/renderer/src/contexts/IFrameContext.tsx line 30 Why it exists. The renderer only dispatches read-file , save-file , and register-plugin messages from iframes whose event.origin parses to a URL whose hostname is exactly one of these values. Plugin content is served locally through the plugin file server (see PLUGIN_FILE_SERVER_PORT , default port 3000), so all legitimate origins are loopback. Any port on those hosts is accepted; the port itself is env-configurable. Security note. The previous implementation used text.startsWith(item) , which would accept attacker-controlled hosts such as http://localhost.evil.example . The current implementation parses event.origin with new URL(...) and compares hostname for exact equality; malformed origins fall through to a deny. Landed in [PR #109][pr-109]. User-visible behavior. Any plugin iframe served from a non-loopback origin is silently ignored: its messages never trigger file reads, writes, or registration. When to reconsider. Add an entry only if you deliberately host plugin content off-device (for example, over https:// to a controlled host). Broadening this list widens the file-read and file-write surface exposed to third-party pages, and non-loopback additions should use exact origin equality against a full URL, not just a hostname.

docs.text: Symbol: SLICE_RENDER_PROPORTION Value: 0.008 Source: src/renderer/src/routes/SlicesPage/SlicesPage.tsx line 26 Why it exists. The 3D slice preview draws only every Nth rectangle where N = floor(rects.length * 0.008) . This keeps very long paths (tens of thousands of rects) from stalling the WebGL scene. User-visible behavior. For a 10 000-rect path this renders roughly 125 rectangles: enough to convey the shape of the sweep without freezing the visualization. Fewer rects than about 125 render every rect. When to reconsider. Raise it to see more slices in the preview at the cost of frame rate; lower it if the preview lags on very long paths.
